newsitem.title: USA: Calif. owes $14.1 bln on general obligations- Gov..
newsitem.headline: Calif. owes $14.1 bln on general obligations- Gov..

text.p: California Gov. Pete Wilson said Thursday that the state currently owes $14.1 billion in principal on authorized general obligation bonds.

The cost to the state's general fund for the payment of interest and redemption on these bonds was $1.911 billion in 1995-1996, and was estimated to be $1.953 billion in 1996-1997 and $1.979 billion in 1997-1998, the governor said.

Outstanding lease revenue bonds totaled $5.845 billion as of June 30, 1996 and were expected to total $6.398 billion as of June 30, 1997 and $7.102 billion by June 30, 1998, according to Wilson's 1997-1998 budget summary.
The cost to the state's general fund for lease payments was $482.8 million in 1995-1996 and was projected to be $542.6 million in 1996-1997 and $593.3 million for 1997-1998.

Using the most common measure of bonded indebtedness -- the ratio of net tax-supported debt to general fund revenues -- California's debt ratio came to 5.3 percent in 1996-1997, according to Wilson's budget summary.
Using this measure, California's debt would rise to a maximum of 5.5 percent in 1998-1999 if no other bonds are authorized.

The debt measure would rise to 5.7 percent in 1999-2000 if the bond programs proposed in Wilson's budget are implemented, including $2 billion for schools, $200 million for the infrastructure bank and $93 million for various lease revenue projects.
